François Truffaut. A French New Wave director and influential film critic who championed the auteur theory and turned it into praxis through intimate, character-driven films about human vulnerability and memory. His breakthrough The 400 Blows established him as the movement's humanist pole, opposite Godard's formalism, and he sustained a career of elegant, melancholic explorations of love, regret, and childhood.

Truffaut wrote for Cahiers du cinéma where he developed the auteur theory—the claim that a film's director is its primary creative author, akin to a novelist's authorship. He directed The 400 Blows in 1959, a semi-autobiographical coming-of-age film that introduced actor Jean-Pierre Léaud and the New Wave aesthetic. He created the Antoine Doinel series across four films from 1959 to 1979, following the same character through adulthood—a radical act of longitudinal narrative cinema.

Known for direct, handheld camera work, natural lighting, and scenes shot in real locations rather than sets, he frequently worked with cinematographer Raoul Coutard and composer Georges Delerue, creating a recognisable visual and sonic palette. He made Day for Night in 1973, a film about filmmaking itself—a late-career meditation on cinema's illusory nature. His final film, Confidentially Yours in 1983, remains tender and formally playful despite his declining health.

Truffaut was a fellow New Wave pioneer with Jean-Luc Godard and a Cahiers critic representing opposite aesthetic poles, with Truffaut the humanist and Godard the formalist. He was a co-founder of the nouvelle vague's narrative-focused aesthetic. He shared with Jacques Demy the role of contemporary lyricist-filmmaker, both favouring romantic, introspective narratives. Jean-Pierre Léaud was his muse and the Antoine Doinel alter ego across the series.
